article_title: Learner Response System: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Meg Wiggins, Mary Sawtell and Dr John Jerrim. (2017). Learner Response System: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: LRS theory of change: instant two-way formative feedback improves pace and quality of feedback
description: The Edge Hill developers' logic model holds that timely, focused feedback facilitates learning: pupils respond to questions and are instantly told whether they erred, with suggestions for rectifying mistakes, while teachers receive aggregated feedback on each learner's progress, timing, attempts, and errors so they can adjust within the lesson and target struggling pupils. The report states "The LRS approach is based on the premise that timely and focused feedback is a powerful tool to facilitate learning". The trial tested this mechanism and found no measurable KS2 attainment benefit.
requirements: Teachers must become competent in using all key features of the system and deliver lessons using the handsets in at least three sessions a week, per the developers' logic model
An IT system that runs the software effectively, good ICT support at school level, and expert LRS support sufficient to help even the least confident teachers
constraints: The trial found no evidence of improved KS2 maths or reading results for either cohort, even in high-usage schools
Teachers and pupils noted the system could not let children show their working and occasionally gave negative feedback to wholly or partially correct answers
target_learners: Year 5 and Year 6 primary school pupils in England (aged 9-11), in schools with high proportions of pupils ever eligible for free school meals
target_learning_goals: Key Stage 2 maths and reading attainment
Improved pace and quality of classroom feedback and formative assessment
examples: Teachers used ad hoc and pre-prepared questions with aggregated results displayed on the whiteboard, and self-paced question sets with automatic differentiation and a results timeline showing who was getting questions right or wrong
key_sources: Meg Wiggins, Mary Sawtell and Dr John Jerrim. (2017). Learner Response System: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED581136

article_title: Watch the Moon, Learn the Moon: Lunar Geology Research at School Level with Telescope and Open Source Data
citation: Kevin J. Luke, Abhinav Mishra, Vihaan Ghare, Shaurya Chanyal, Priyamvada Shukla, Anushreya Pandey, Vaishnavi Rane, Ashadieeyah Pathan, Parv Vaja, Sai Gogate, Shreyansh Tiwari, Jagruti Singh, Dhruv Davda. (2024). Watch the Moon, Learn the Moon: Lunar Geology Research at School Level with Telescope and Open Source Data. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01856
title: LROC quickmap open-access lunar data platform as a school science-education resource
description: The LROC quickmap website hosts data products from the LRO and Kaguya missions that the project used extensively, including WAC and NAC imagery, LOLA/Kaguya terrain elevation and slope data, Diviner regolith temperature data and Kaguya iron oxide abundance data. The article describes it as "a powerful tool, offering an unprecedented level of detail about the Moon's surface", from high resolution imagery to topographic maps, and guides students to analyze it individually to foster critical thinking and data interpretation skills.
requirements: Internet access to the quickmap website hosted by Arizona State University
examples: Students pulled terrain elevation, slope, regolith temperature and iron oxide layers for their assigned zones directly from quickmap
key_sources: Kevin J. Luke, Abhinav Mishra, Vihaan Ghare, Shaurya Chanyal, Priyamvada Shukla, Anushreya Pandey, Vaishnavi Rane, Ashadieeyah Pathan, Parv Vaja, Sai Gogate, Shreyansh Tiwari, Jagruti Singh, Dhruv Davda. (2024). Watch the Moon, Learn the Moon: Lunar Geology Research at School Level with Telescope and Open Source Data. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01856

article_title: Q-BEAST: A Practical Course on Experimental Evaluation and Characterization of Quantum Computing Systems
citation: Minh Chung, Yaknan Gambo, Burak Mete, Xiao-Ting Michelle To, Florian Krötz, Korbinian Staudacher, Martin Letras, Xiaolong Deng, Mounika Vavilala, Amir Raoofy, Jorge Echavarria, Luigi Iapichino, Laura Schulz, Josef Weidendorfer, Martin Schulz. (2025). Q-BEAST: A Practical Course on Experimental Evaluation and Characterization of Quantum Computing Systems. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.14084
title: LRZ quantum backend fleet and QLM emulator available to Q-BEAST students
description: Students experiment with multiple quantum backends: simulators, the QLM (Quantum Learning Machine from Eviden, known as Qaptiva HPC) emulator 'capable of state-vector simulations up to 38 qubits in double precision', three IQM superconducting devices (Q5, Q20, and the 20-qubit production system QExa20), and an AQT trapped-ion device (AQT20). Survey data showed the most frequently used backends were QC simulator, QLM, and QExa20 because of their availability.
requirements: Backend access through MQSS and shared quantum resource allocation slots
constraints: Other systems were used less often partly due to construction work, maintenance, software updates, and busy job queues shared between users and research groups
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate students running quantum experiments
target_learning_goals: comparing simulator, emulator, and real quantum hardware behaviour
examples: Figure 5 reports student feedback on access frequency across the six backend options, with QC simulator, QLM, and QExa20 most used in the often and very often groups
key_sources: Minh Chung, Yaknan Gambo, Burak Mete, Xiao-Ting Michelle To, Florian Krötz, Korbinian Staudacher, Martin Letras, Xiaolong Deng, Mounika Vavilala, Amir Raoofy, Jorge Echavarria, Luigi Iapichino, Laura Schulz, Josef Weidendorfer, Martin Schulz. (2025). Q-BEAST: A Practical Course on Experimental Evaluation and Characterization of Quantum Computing Systems. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.14084
